lawyer: BM Alauddin, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners.
parties:
Abdul Jalil and six others ------ Petitioners
vs
State and another ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment: 7. There had been a drastice change of the Code since the passing of the Law Reforms Ordinance 1978. For the last 15 (fifteen) years, the basic structure and character of the Code had been altered. In this connection reference may be made to the provision of the Code relating to the release of the accused if the police fails to complete the investigation and submit the report or the Court fails to complete the trial within a certain time, the revival of the case where the accused stood released, omission of the warrant procedure, the discharge of the accused under section 241A or 265C of the Code, the dealing with a petition of complaint by the Magistrate in a case triable by the court of Sessions, the omission of enquiry under Chapter XVIII, the trial of the accused in his absence, the introduction of section 439A and appeals by the complainant in a complaint case on matters of law only and appeals against inadequacy of sentence by the State and the complainant and the amendment of section 439(4). The drastic changes in the Code had altered the basic structure and character of the Code. In this connection we want to say a few words of the trial of the accused in his absence. The principle of criminal jurisprudence or the principle of natural justice requires that the accused be identified on the dock by the witnesses least there is a massacre of justice. But now trial of the accused in his absence is a normal affair. But neither the High Court Division nor the Appellate Division (the apex, Court) had struck down the provisions relating to trial in the absence of the accused. The identification of the accused on the dock is very vital for the administration of criminal justice. The absentia trial has made the examination of the accused under section 342 completely redundant. In this connection there are many appeals now pending in this Court against the order of conviction and sentence passed in trials held in the absence of the accused on the ground that the accused did not know about the case, etc. In such cases many appeals had been filed after 3/5 years out of time with applications under section 5 of the Limitation Act. This shows how much vital it is for criminal trial that the accused be identified on the dock. Could this Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the accused merely on the ground that the accused was tried in his absence, without declaring that the provisions relating to absentia trial being against the principle of natural justice or fundamental principle of criminal justice be struck down? Could such a matter be remediable under section 561A of the Code? This clearly shows that such relief cannot be given under section 561A of the Code inasmuch as the relevant provisions of the Code permit atrial in the absence of the accused. In other words, where there is an express provision in the Code barring the exercise of a particular jurisdiction (as under section 439) of this Court the jurisdiction may not be exercised under a general provision of the Code as under section 561A of the Code.
